Moved to suspend standing and sessional orders to delay debate on the Migration Amendment (Temporary Sponsored Visas) Bill 2013 until a full research report on 457 visa abuse, industry consultation, and a regulatory impact statement on the proposed labour market testing were completed, accusing the government of rushing the bill through for the unions before the election.

Opposed the Migration Amendment (Temporary Sponsored Visas) Bill 2013 as a union-driven attack on skilled migration, citing department official Wendy Southern's evidence that no advice supported the minister's claim of 10,000 rorts, noting there were 108,810 primary 457 visa holders as at 30 April 2013, and quoting demographer Peter McDonald calling the Prime Minister's rhetoric on the issue nasty.

Supported the 457 visa bill, describing a constituent tradesperson who lost a job to a 457 visa worker, cited figures showing 457 visa numbers rose from 68,400 in June 2010 to 106,680 in May 2013, a 56 per cent increase, and noted a Migration Council survey found 15 per cent of employers admitted they could have hired locally, while the bill extends the period for a displaced visa holder to find new work from 28 to 90 days.

Called the 457 visa bill the most racist legislation he had encountered in parliament, comparing it to anti-Chinese hostility at the Lambing Flat goldfields riots 150 years earlier, and quoted the immigration minister's own maiden speech about not wanting his race to be an election issue.

Accused the shadow minister for immigration of stoking ethnic division during debate on the Migration Amendment (Temporary Sponsored Visas) Bill 2013, after he warned a particular ethnic group would be victimised by a 457 visa crackdown having grown by 17 per cent through such visas, and recalled the shadow minister's earlier comments linking a rape case to refugee claimants.

Opposed the Migration Amendment (Temporary Sponsored Visas) Bill 2013, accusing the union movement, which represents only 13 per cent of the private sector workforce, of controlling Labor Party policy, and defended 457 visa holders, noting more than 108,000 people held one as of April 2013 and 70 per cent worked in professional or managerial roles.

Opposed the Migration Amendment (Temporary Sponsored Visas) Bill 2013, arguing it was rushed through to please the union movement and to distract from a chaotic border protection regime, contrasting the government's swift action on 457 visas with its months-long inaction on the Houston inquiry's recommendation to excise the mainland.

Opposed the Migration Amendment (Temporary Sponsored Visas) Bill, disputing the immigration minister's unsubstantiated claim of 10,000 rorted 457 visas, noting union leader Tony Sheldon reported only 24 complaints in 12 months with none referred to the department, and said 457 visa numbers had risen by just 1.7 per cent over the past year.

Opposed the migration bill, calling it the 'City West Water Bill' after a union picket over 457 visa workers at a Werribee water project, noted 24 complaints in 12 months with none referred to the immigration department, and praised former minister Chris Bowen for intervening to let a group of Chinese 457 workers stay in Warrnambool after more than five years at a local abattoir.

Supported the migration bill, citing a Migration Council survey finding 15 per cent of employers used 457 visas despite reporting no difficulty finding local labour, and pointed to the Northern Co-operative Meat Co. abattoir in the Page electorate, which employs nearly a thousand workers, as a model combining 457 visas with local training.

Opposed the migration bill as hypocritical, citing a 2011 joint press release from Labor's own tourism and immigration ministers acknowledging a tourism skills shortage needing 457 visas, and said Labor had cut compliance funding for 457 monitoring by more than $20 million, a 30 per cent reduction, in government.

Announced opposition to the migration bill, arguing existing sponsorship obligations already carry penalties of up to AUD51,000 per breach for a corporation, and said a 20 per cent rise in 457 visas against about 1.1 per cent growth in the construction industry was not evidence of rorting, only of laws needing to be enforced rather than replaced.

Opposed the 457 visa bill, noting the program was introduced by the Howard government in 1996 to address skills shortages, said the minister could not substantiate his claim of 10,000 abuse cases, and cited figures showing India accounted for about 20.5 per cent of 457 visa grants in 2012-13.

Opposed the 457 visa bill on behalf of Riverina farmers, citing grain grower Mark Hoskinson's reliance on French agricultural students for his harvest, and noted the bill would extend the period for a displaced 457 worker to find new sponsorship from 28 to 98 days while new compliance inspectors would cost $3.4 million.

Opposed the 457 visa bill, saying the minister admitted plucking his claimed 10,000 abuse cases from thin air, cited a joint industry letter from the Australian Industry Group, Business Council of Australia and Migration Council Australia warning against the changes, and said 12,700 people had arrived by unauthorised boat this year, three times the same period last year, bringing the total under Labor to more than 44,600.

Opposed the 457 visa bill, noting the government could face an election in 86 days, recounted how then immigration minister Chris Bowen approved a migration agreement for a Gina Rinehart mining project, and said the South Australian Labor government was reportedly the state's biggest user of 457 visas.

Opposed the 457 visa bill as a protectionist measure driven by the union movement, citing CFMEU official Dave Noonan's claim that the proportion of 457 visas granted onshore had grown from 43 per cent to 51 per cent in a year, noted labour market testing was tried from 1996 and dropped by the Howard government in 2001 as unworkable, and said the minister's claim of 10,000 abuse cases remained unsubstantiated.

Opposed the 457 visa bill, reading a constituent's email from Bicycle Entrepreneur owner Michael D'Arcy in Belmont describing his inability to source bicycle mechanics locally, noted the WA government was lobbying for 16,500 regional sponsored visas, and compared the changes to the 2007-08 weakening of border protection that preceded more than 40,000 boat arrivals and over 1,000 deaths at sea.

Opposed the Migration Amendment (Temporary Sponsored Visas) Bill 2013, citing a Freedom of Information finding that the immigration minister had no evidence for a claimed 10,000 rorts of the 457 visa scheme, noted Western Australia's 457 applications fell 6.4 per cent in 2012 to 2013, and criticised extending the job-seeking period from 28 to 90 days as unhelpful red tape.

Opposed the bill, describing how 457 visa holders from the Philippines have revitalised piggeries and schools around Yarrawalla in northern Victoria, and said about 30 or 40 per cent of skilled migrants historically went on to become Australian citizens under the coalition, disputing claims the visa system was being widely rorted.

Opposed the bill, recalling only four people were in immigration detention when Labor was elected in 2007, and said since 2008 more than 700 boats carrying over 44,200 people have arrived illegally, at a cost exceeding $10 billion to taxpayers.

Argued that the Migration Amendment (Temporary Sponsored Visas) Bill 2013 was based on a false premise and would burden employers through labour-market testing and increased compliance requirements. Supported skilled temporary migration, called for evidence, consultation and a regulatory impact statement, and said the coalition would oppose the bill and seek committee referral.

Argued that the Migration Amendment (Temporary Sponsored Visas) Bill 2013 would impose unnecessary regulation on employers, lacked evidence of widespread abuse, and threatened Australia's skilled migration program. Supported the 457 visa scheme as vital for addressing skills gaps, criticised labour-market testing, and said the bill risked dividing Australians and undermining economic growth.

Argued that the bill would add unnecessary regulation to the 457 visa program and was not supported by evidence of widespread abuse. Cited regional skills shortages and problems affecting businesses, supported extending the period to find new sponsored employment from 28 days to 90 days, and said the coalition would oppose the bill.

Moved the Intellectual Property Laws Amendment Bill 2013, clarifying Crown use provisions for patents in areas like health care, implementing the TRIPS protocol to let Australian manufacturers export generic medicines to developing countries citing a UN estimate that 260 million people were infected with malaria, HIV or tuberculosis in 2010 resulting in 3.6 million deaths, and establishing a first-of-its-kind single trans-Tasman patent examination and attorney regulation system with New Zealand.

Argued that the Intellectual Property Laws Amendment Bill 2013 was rushed, poorly drafted and inadequately scrutinised despite its acceptable objectives. Raised concerns about Crown use, compulsory licences, the Australia-US FTA, TRIPS obligations, consultation and committee processes, and urged the government to withdraw and redraft the bill.

Supported the Intellectual Property Laws Amendment Bill 2013 as an improvement to the patent system, particularly through clearer Crown use provisions, compulsory licensing for exporting medicines, plant breeders' rights reforms and a trans-Tasman patent attorney regime. Criticised patents over human genes and reported the United States Supreme Court decision on BRCA gene patents.

Opposed the Intellectual Property Laws Amendment Bill 2013 and called for more time and scrutiny, citing its complexity, limited committee consideration and inadequate consultation. Raised concerns about TRIPS provisions, possible unintended consequences, international obligations and rushed legislative processes.

In parliamentary jargon, they voted to read the bill for a [second time](https://www.peo.gov.au/learning/fact-sheets/making-a-law.html). the Senate will now discuss the bill in more detail. ### What is the bill's main idea? The [bill](http://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id:legislation/billhome/r5074) was introduced to establish the Early Years Quality Fund Special Account to: > *provide $300 million over two years to approved centre based long day care services in the form of grants to be used exclusively for the remuneration of employees and other employment-related costs and expenses.* Read more in the [bills digest](https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/bd/bd1213a/13bd133).
John Hogg The question now is that the remaining stages of the bill be agreed to and the bill be now passed.

Argued for the Early Years Quality Fund Special Account Bill 2013, defending the $300 million fund to raise wages for long day care educators through enterprise agreements, citing a further $190 million already invested in workforce qualifications, and condemning commentator Judith Sloan's description of educators as dimwits.

Opposed the Early Years Quality Fund Special Account Bill 2013, arguing it bypasses the Fair Work Commission and pressures childcare centres into enterprise bargaining agreements to access $300 million in funding, and said only 76 per cent of women aged 25 to 54 are in paid work in Australia, compared with over 80 per cent elsewhere.

Opposed the Early Years Quality Fund Special Account Bill 2013, calling it a farce that will lift wages for only 30 to 40 per cent of long day care workers over two years, and cited reports that centres were told 60 per cent of staff must join the union to access the $300 million fund.

Supported the Early Years Quality Fund Special Account Bill 2013, citing a $25 billion four-year investment in early childhood education and care, wage increases of $3 an hour for Certificate III qualified educators, and research showing 90 per cent of a child's brain development occurs in the early years.

Opposed the Early Years Quality Fund Special Account Bill 2013 as unaffordable, noting the government's cumulative deficits of $172 billion, and cited the Australian Industry Group's objection that conditioning funding on enterprise agreements is unfair and could breach section 344 of the Fair Work Act.

Argued against the Early Years Quality Fund Special Account Bill 2013, accepting its wage-support objective but contending that it bypassed the Fair Work Commission, was rushed through parliament, benefited only about 40 per cent of childcare workers, provided funding for two years, and would increase costs for parents.

Opposed the Early Years Quality Fund Special Account Bill 2013, arguing that a rushed inquiry and selective two-year funding would divide childcare workers and services, disadvantage regional and rural centres, and create higher fees, staff poaching, and uncertainty after funding ceased.

Opposed the Early Years Quality Fund Special Account Bill 2013, arguing that its $300 million fund would support only 30 to 40 per cent of long day care workers for two years, exclude many regional and rural services, create a two-tier system, and force centres and families to absorb higher wage costs.

Opposed the Early Years Quality Fund Special Account Bill 2013, arguing that its $300 million fund would benefit only around 30 to 40 per cent of long day care workers for two years, create a wage divide, and improperly bypass the Fair Work Commission.

Argued that quality childcare was increasingly unaffordable for families and that the bill's $300 million, two-year wage fund would pass further costs to families while attaching funding conditions concerning union membership.

Summed up the Early Years Quality Fund bill, saying the government would invest a record $25 billion over four years in early childhood education, including $300 million over two years in grants to supplement educators' wages, and announced a new Pay Equity Unit within the Fair Work Commission.

The speaker moved a motion to set the Senate's sitting hours for 28 June 2013 from 9:30 am to 3:40 pm, with specific time allocations for general business notice no. 1288 (relating to the Committee of Privileges) and for government business including the Early Years Quality Fund Special Account Bill 2013 and the Migration Amendment (Temporary Sponsored Visas) Bill 2013, each with limited debate time.

The government introduced the Early Years Quality Fund Special Account Bill 2013, establishing a $300 million fund to support wage increases for early childhood educators and assist with implementing the National Quality Framework. The opposition argued the fund would benefit fewer than 40% of childcare workers, primarily served union membership drives, and created a two-tiered system.

Supported the Banking Amendment (Unclaimed Money) Bill 2013 as a fix to the government's own earlier changes, which cut the unclaimed-money period for bank and life insurance accounts from seven to three years and for superannuation from five years to 12 months, expected to raise nearly $900 million over four years, and cited a Brisbane woman losing more than $150,000 and a pensioner losing $22,000 under the changes.

Supported the Banking Amendment (Unclaimed Money) Bill 2013 as a fix for a policy failure, saying the change to a three-year unclaimed-money period raised an extra $93.4 million from bank accounts and $513.5 million from superannuation in 2012-13, for a total of $700.9 million, and argued the government pursued it to mask a $19.4 billion budget deficit.

Argued that the Banking Amendment (Unclaimed Money) Bill 2013 corrected rushed legislation by excluding reactivated accounts from transfer to the Commonwealth and allowing refunds to authorised deposit-taking institutions. Criticised the government's use of unclaimed funds to support its budget position and cited warnings that banks needed more time to implement the changes.

Argued that the bill corrected rushed unclaimed-money legislation that had appropriated funds from bank, life insurance and superannuation accounts to support the budget. Said the changes could affect savers, families and older people, and supported amendments to prevent transfers from reactivated accounts and address refund problems.

Argued that the bill corrected unclaimed-money changes that had shortened periods for bank, life insurance and superannuation accounts and transferred funds into government revenue. Supported delaying implementation so banks and financial institutions could establish proper governance and said coalition amendments were defeated.

Argued that the bill addressed technical flaws requiring authorised deposit-taking institutions to transfer money even after an account had been reactivated. Said the amendments would exclude such accounts and permit repayment to institutions that had used their own funds, while criticising the earlier legislation as rushed and poorly drafted.

Said the bill represented another attempt to take money from bank accounts that had not been active for three years. Referred to a report about a pensioner's account established for funeral costs and argued that the policy amounted to unfair seizure of unclaimed money.

Criticised the unclaimed money changes, recounting a Queensland pensioner whose bank balance fell from $22,600 to zero after the government took his account while he recovered from heart bypass surgery, and cited $172 billion in accumulated budget deficits and a debt cap raised four times from $75 billion to $300 billion.

Said the coalition would support the Banking Amendment (Unclaimed Money) Bill 2013 because it allows the government to refund money wrongly taken from reactivated accounts, but condemned the underlying policy as unprincipled, noting the deficit blew out from a forecast $7 billion to $19 billion and gross debt reached $300 billion with a $12 billion annual interest bill.

Welcomed a 70-68 defeat of the government's attempt to shut down debate on the Banking Amendment (Unclaimed Money) Bill 2013, criticised a separate attempt to ram through 457 visa changes without consultation or a regulatory impact statement, and said Peter Costello remains the greatest Treasurer Australia has had.

Rose to speak on the Banking Amendment (Unclaimed Money) Bill 2013 but first paid tribute to three retiring members whose valedictory statements he had just witnessed, praising them as honourable role models.

Opposed the Banking Amendment (Unclaimed Money) Bill 2013, calling the seizure of dormant funds after just three years a form of theft to offset the government's $340 billion to $350 billion debt, citing an 86-year-old pensioner whose $8,000 funeral savings were stripped and an expected government revenue of a little over $900 million.

Opposed the Banking Amendment (Unclaimed Money) Bill 2013 as a money grab expected to raise about $700 million in 2012-13, citing pensioners' funeral savings and superannuation accounts under $2,000 being swept into consolidated revenue, and asked the minister to detail the bureaucratic cost of processing refund claims.

Argued for the Banking Amendment (Unclaimed Money) Bill 2013, explaining it exempts reactivated accounts from being transferred to the Commonwealth and lets funds be returned to financial institutions that transferred accounts inappropriately, aiming to reunite more Australians with their money and protect it from fee erosion.

Arthur Sinodinos It is a pleasure to give this speech while you are in the chair, Madam Acting Deputy President. There are some of us who hope you may in fact return at some stage. Trish Crossin Thank you. Arthur Sinodinos The Public Governance, Performance and Accountability Bill 2013 proposes to replace the existing model for Commonwealth financial management established through the Financial Management and Accountability Act 1987—the FMA Act—and the Commonwealth Authorities and Companies Act 1997—the CAC Act. It would consolidate under one piece of legislation the governance, performance and accountability requirements for the Commonwealth and relevant entities, which are covered currently under both the FMA and CAC acts. The bill would introduce a new framework for the finances of the Commonwealth, impacting on some 195 entities and around 300,000 individuals who work with them. So this is not a reform to be taken lightly or a reform to be driven by undue haste. Yet, in the dying days of this parliament—for the benefit of those in the gallery—we are being asked to approve a complex bill on which we are provided with a framework but no rules as to how the bill will actually impact, in practice, on the operation of Commonwealth entities. We are talking about entities that cover the management and accountability for revenue and expenses of over $350 billion—that is your money, taxpayers' money—as well as assets of over $390 billion, which are your assets, and liabilities of over $640 billion—liabilities that we have rung up in your name. This type of reform is precisely the sort of reform that should be covered by a new parliament regardless of its colour or stripe. Most appropriately, this bill has been subject to an inquiry by the Joint Committee of Public Accounts and Audit. Two fundamental concerns have been identified: the lack of detail as to how the new financial framework would actually be applied, and the unnecessary haste with which it is being brought be

Introduced the Public Governance, Performance and Accountability Bill 2013 to replace the Financial Management and Accountability Act and the Commonwealth Authorities and Companies Act, both in place since 1998, following the Commonwealth Financial Accountability Review announced on 8 December 2010, establishing a single principles-based framework covering duties, planning, risk management, cooperation and accountability across all Commonwealth entities.

The Selection of Bills Committee report recommended referring the Australian Jobs Bill 2013, Export Market Development Grants Amendment Bill 2013, Private Health Insurance Legislation Amendment (Base Premium) Bill 2013, and Public Governance, Performance and Accountability Bill 2013 to specific committees for inquiry by June 2013, and recommended not referring several other bills including the DisabilityCare Australia Fund Bill 2013 and related tax bills; the report was adopted.

Opposed the Public Governance, Performance and Accountability Bill 2013 in the Senate, noting it would cover 195 entities and around 300,000 employees managing revenue and expenses of more than $350 billion, and cited the Auditor-General's concerns that the bill's detailed rules had not been exposed for proper consultation before being rushed through parliament.

Opposed the Public Governance, Performance and Accountability Bill 2013 as lacking detail, noting the number of Commonwealth agencies has grown from 87 to 107 in five years while GDP grew 64 per cent between 2001 and 2009 against 98 per cent growth in government expenditure, and cited a 2010 review finding 63 agencies with fewer than 500 employees ripe for rationalisation.

Closed debate on the Public Governance, Performance and Accountability Bill 2013, confirming that detailed rules developed from the December 2010 review will be open for public comment for at least 30 days, and that the act itself will be independently reviewed after three years.

Urged parliament to pass the Public Interest Disclosure Bill 2013 in its final two weeks, citing the Australian whistleblower protection standard AS 8004-2003 and noting Queensland passed similar legislation in September and October 2010, after three years of negotiation on the federal bill.

A revised explanatory memorandum for the Public Governance, Performance and Accountability Bill 2013 was tabled, with the bill to be listed separately on the Notice Paper after the second reading debate is adjourned. The bill and related bills were read a first time together without formalities.

The coalition opposed the Public Governance, Performance and Accountability Bill 2013, arguing it was being rushed through parliament without the necessary detail or consultation, despite the Auditor-General and other officials recommending more time. The speaker supported the bill’s principles but opposed its passage, warning that key rules had not been drafted and that haste risked mismanagement of over $350 billion in revenue and $640 billion in liabilities.
The Public Governance, Performance and Accountability Bill 2013 passed its third reading.
